topics.name: Mohorovičić discontinuity
topics.kicker: Boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle · Found by seismology in 1909
topics.briefing: In 1909, the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić noticed that waves from an earthquake near Zagreb reached faraway stations sooner than expected, as if they had sped up underground. He had found the boundary where Earth’s crust ends and the denser mantle begins, now called the Mohorovičić discontinuity, or “Moho.” It lies only about 5 to 10 kilometers below the ocean floor but much deeper under the continents.
topics.answerHtml: Mohorovičić discontinuity (accept Moho or crust–mantle boundary; prompt on discontinuity or boundary; do not accept “Gutenberg discontinuity,” “Conrad discontinuity,” or “Mohs scale”)
accept: boundary between the crust and mantle
boundary between the crust and the mantle

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Novelist John Steinbeck wrote a _Life_ magazine article about a 1961 test drilling for a project that hoped to bore through the ocean floor all the way to this boundary. Congress canceled that project, Project Mohole, in 1966.
tossups.r: Seismic waves speed up as they cross this boundary. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle, discovered by a Croatian seismologist in 1909.

tossups.p: Walter Munk and Harry Hess belonged to a joke-named group, the American Miscellaneous Society, that proposed drilling down to this boundary in 1957. Their project’s name combined this boundary’s nickname with the word “hole.”
tossups.r: This boundary lies only about 5 to 10 kilometers below the ocean floor. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: In many places, a shallower boundary named for the seismologist Victor Conrad splits the continental crust into an upper and a lower layer, both of which lie above this deeper boundary. Beneath most continents, this deeper boundary lies around 35 kilometers down.
tossups.r: Below this boundary lies dense, olivine-rich peridotite. For 10 points, name this boundary where Earth’s crust ends and the mantle begins.

tossups.p: Geologists map how deep this boundary lies by setting off explosions, or shaking the ground with heavy vibrating trucks, and timing the waves that bounce back up from it like echoes. The waves bounce back because the rock below this boundary is denser and carries them faster.
tossups.r: This boundary is much deeper beneath continents than beneath the ocean floor. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: In Oman’s Samail ophiolite, a huge slice of ancient seafloor shoved up onto land, geologists can walk across this boundary, stepping from gabbro onto peridotite. Such exposures are rare, because this boundary is usually buried kilometers deep.
tossups.r: Seismic waves speed up as they cross this boundary from the crust into the mantle. For 10 points, name this boundary discovered in 1909 by a Croatian scientist.

tossups.p: Japan’s deep-sea drilling ship Chikyu, whose name means “Earth,” was designed with the goal of drilling all the way down to this boundary beneath the seafloor. No drill has ever reached this boundary.
tossups.r: Below this boundary, P-waves jump to about 8 kilometers per second. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: Seismologists call P-waves that race along just beneath this boundary head waves and label them Pn. At faraway stations, those waves arrive before waves that take the shorter route through the rock above it.
tossups.r: This boundary separates the crust from the mantle beneath it. For 10 points, name this boundary, which has a four-letter nickname.

tossups.p: This boundary lies deepest beneath Tibet and the Himalayas, around 70 kilometers down, because tall mountains are held up by deep roots of light rock, much as most of an iceberg hides underwater.
tossups.r: Beneath the ocean floor, it lies only about 5 to 10 kilometers down. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: Seismometers left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts detected a lunar version of this boundary a few dozen kilometers below the surface. On Earth, the rock gabbro often lies just above this boundary beneath the oceans.
tossups.r: Seismic waves speed up sharply as they cross this boundary. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle, discovered in 1909.

tossups.p: Geologists distinguish a “seismic” version of this boundary, defined by a jump in the speed of earthquake waves, from a “petrologic” version, defined by a change in rock type. The two versions do not always line up exactly.
tossups.r: Below this boundary lies dense, olivine-rich peridotite. For 10 points, name this boundary where Earth’s crust ends and the mantle begins.

tossups.p: This boundary’s discoverer was also a meteorologist who directed the weather observatory in Zagreb and equipped it with seismographs. He found this boundary by studying records of an October 1909 earthquake in the nearby Kupa Valley.
tossups.r: Seismic waves speed up as they cross this boundary. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle, named for a Croatian scientist.

tossups.p: The Soviet Union’s Kola Superdeep Borehole reached more than 12 kilometers down, making it the deepest hole ever drilled, yet it never came close to this boundary, which lies much deeper beneath continents.
tossups.r: Beneath the ocean floor, this boundary lies only about 5 to 10 kilometers down. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: Records of an October 1909 earthquake in Croatia’s Kupa Valley showed two sets of waves reaching distant stations: slower ones that had stayed in the shallow rock above this boundary, and faster ones that had dipped below it.
tossups.r: It is named for the Croatian seismologist who found it. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: P-waves speed up from roughly 6 or 7 kilometers per second to about 8 when they cross this boundary, a jump that reveals denser rock below. That denser rock is mostly olivine-rich peridotite.
tossups.r: This boundary lies much deeper beneath continents than beneath the ocean floor. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle.

tossups.p: This boundary lies within the rigid lithosphere rather than at its base, so moving plates carry it along with them. Crustal rocks such as granite and basalt lie above this boundary, while dense, olivine-rich peridotite lies just below it.
tossups.r: Seismic waves speed up as they cross it. For 10 points, name this boundary between Earth’s crust and mantle, discovered by a Croatian seismologist in 1909.

trap.title: Which boundary is which?
trap.body: Earth’s interior has several named boundaries, and quiz bowl asks about each one. The Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) separates the crust from the mantle, the Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle from the outer core about 2,900 kilometers down, and the Conrad discontinuity lies inside the continental crust. Players also mix up the Moho with the Mohs hardness scale, which ranks minerals and has nothing to do with Earth’s layers.
trap.fix: Crust above and mantle below, 1909, a Croatian scientist, Project Mohole, or waves jumping to about 8 kilometers per second mean the Moho. The core, the S-wave shadow zone, or about 2,900 kilometers down mean the Gutenberg discontinuity. Saying only “discontinuity” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Mohorovičić discontinuity (accept Moho; prompt on discontinuity; do not accept “Gutenberg discontinuity”)

topics.name: Ocean currents
topics.kicker: Steady flows of seawater · Carry heat around the globe and shape climate
topics.dates: Gulf Stream noted by Ponce de León in 1513
topics.briefing: Ocean currents are like rivers inside the sea: huge, steady flows of water that can carry heat thousands of kilometers. The warm Gulf Stream carries tropical heat north along the U.S. East Coast and on toward Europe, while cold, deep currents creep along the seafloor in a slow loop nicknamed the “global conveyor belt.” Winds, Earth’s spin, and differences in temperature and saltiness keep them moving.
topics.answerHtml: Ocean currents (accept currents, oceanic currents, or ocean circulation; accept surface or deep currents; prompt on thermohaline circulation; do not accept “tides,” “waves,” “gyres,” “upwelling,” or one named current like the “Gulf Stream”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The volume of water moved by these flows is measured in sverdrups, each equal to one million cubic meters per second, a unit named for Norwegian oceanographer Harald Sverdrup. The one that circles Antarctica moves more sverdrups than any other.
tossups.r: Surface examples are pushed mainly by the wind. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater, such as the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: Vagn Walfrid Ekman showed that wind-driven seawater turns more and more with depth in a spiral, so the overall movement of the water is 90 degrees to the right of the wind in the Northern Hemisphere.
tossups.r: Earth’s spin also deflects these flows through the Coriolis effect. For 10 points, name these steady movements of seawater, like the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: Fridtjof Nansen let his ship _Fram_ freeze into Arctic sea ice so that these flows would carry it across the polar sea, and he noticed the ice drifting to the right of the wind. That observation inspired Vagn Walfrid Ekman’s famous spiral.
tossups.r: In the Northern Hemisphere, these flows form giant clockwise loops called gyres. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: In 1948, Henry Stommel explained why these flows run fastest and narrowest along the western edges of ocean basins, an effect called western intensification. Japan’s Kuroshio [“koo-roh-SHEE-oh”], whose name means “Black Tide,” is a classic example of that effect.
tossups.r: Another example, the warm Gulf Stream, flows up the U.S. East Coast. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: In 1513, Juan Ponce de León’s ships off Florida were pushed backward by one of these flows even though the wind filled their sails. His pilot, Antón de Alaminos, later rode that same flow to speed a ship home to Spain.
tossups.r: That flow, the Gulf Stream, later appeared on a chart printed by Benjamin Franklin. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: Geochemist Wallace Broecker popularized the image of a “great ocean conveyor,” a worldwide loop of these flows in which cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and slowly returns to the surface elsewhere over many centuries.
tossups.r: Deep examples are driven by differences in temperature and saltiness. For 10 points, name these flows of seawater, such as the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: After a shipping container of bath toys, including rubber ducks, spilled into the North Pacific in 1992, oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer tracked where the toys washed ashore to learn about these flows. He also tracked a spill of thousands of Nike sneakers.
tossups.r: Plastic trash carried by these flows piles up in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: In 1947, Thor Heyerdahl’s balsa raft _Kon-Tiki_ drifted from Peru to Polynesia, carried by the trade winds and by one of these flows. That cold flow, the Humboldt, feeds some of the world’s biggest anchovy fisheries.
tossups.r: Cold examples like that one help make coastal deserts such as Chile’s Atacama extremely dry. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: Off the coast of East Africa, the Somali flow reverses direction twice a year as the monsoon winds switch, making it one of the few examples of these flows that change course with the seasons.
tossups.r: Surface examples of these flows are pushed mainly by the wind. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater, such as the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: Thousands of robotic Argo floats drift with these flows, sinking deep and then rising to the surface to radio back measurements of temperature and saltiness. Earlier scientists studied these flows by tossing sealed drift bottles into the sea.
tossups.r: The largest example circles Antarctica from west to east. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater, such as the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: Many large examples of these flows are geostrophic [“jee-oh-STROF-ik”], meaning the Coriolis effect balances the push from slight differences in the height of the sea surface. Satellites measure those bumps in the sea surface to map these flows from space.
tossups.r: In the Northern Hemisphere, they form clockwise loops called gyres. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: As one of these flows meanders off the U.S. East Coast, some of its loops pinch off into giant swirling eddies called warm-core and cold-core rings. In the Northern Hemisphere, the warm-core rings spin clockwise and the cold-core rings spin counterclockwise.
tossups.r: That flow, the warm Gulf Stream, helps carry tropical heat toward Europe. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: North Atlantic Deep Water forms where cold, salty water sinks near Greenland, while the densest water of all, Antarctic Bottom Water, sinks near Antarctica. Both feed slow, deep examples of these flows that creep along the seafloor.
tossups.r: That deep worldwide loop is called the “global conveyor belt.” For 10 points, name these flows of seawater, which also include the Gulf Stream.

tossups.p: Where the cold Labrador flow meets warm water from the south off Newfoundland, the Grand Banks are famous for thick fog and rich fishing grounds. The Labrador flow also carries icebergs south from Greenland into busy shipping lanes.
tossups.r: Another cold example, the Humboldt, flows north along South America’s west coast. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin and his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain, printed an early chart of one of these flows to help mail ships cross the Atlantic faster. The Sargasso Sea is the only sea bordered entirely by these flows instead of land.
tossups.r: Earth’s spin bends these flows through the Coriolis effect. For 10 points, name these steady flows of seawater, such as the Gulf Stream.

trap.title: Not just the Gulf Stream
trap.body: Tossups on ocean currents in general love to name famous examples, like the Gulf Stream, the Kuroshio, or the Humboldt, so players blurt out one name, which is wrong. Neighboring answer lines are traps too: tides are the twice-daily rise and fall of the sea caused mostly by the Moon, waves are energy rippling across the surface, gyres are the giant loops that currents form, and upwelling is cold water rising along a coast.
trap.fix: Listen for “these flows” or “these movements of seawater,” and answer “ocean currents” or just “currents.” If a tossup asks for “this circulation” and describes only the slow, deep loop driven by temperature and saltiness, it wants thermohaline circulation; on a general currents tossup, that answer earns only a prompt here.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ocean currents (accept currents; prompt on thermohaline circulation; do not accept “tides,” “waves,” “gyres,” or one named current like the “Gulf Stream”)

topics.name: Bowen’s reaction series
topics.kicker: Order minerals crystallize from cooling magma · Olivine first, quartz last
topics.dates: Worked out by Norman Bowen in the early 1900s
topics.briefing: Bowen’s reaction series is the recipe for how cooling magma turns into rock. In the early 1900s, Canadian scientist Norman Bowen melted samples in a lab furnace and cooled them step by step, and he found that minerals crystallize in a set order: olivine first, at the hottest temperatures, and quartz last. His Y-shaped chart explains why dark basalt and pale granite are made of such different minerals.
topics.answerHtml: Bowen’s reaction series (accept Bowen’s series; prompt on reaction series, Bowen, or one branch, like the discontinuous series; do not accept “Goldich dissolution series” or “fractional crystallization”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Samuel Goldich showed that minerals break down at Earth’s surface in about the same order as this sequence, so the earliest minerals in it weather the fastest. This sequence’s continuous branch is made up of the plagioclase feldspars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that shows the order in which minerals crystallize from cooling magma.

tossups.p: Plagioclase crystals with calcium-rich cores and sodium-rich rims, called zoned crystals, form when magma cools too quickly for them to finish reacting with the melt along one branch of this sequence. That branch is called continuous, because its crystal structure never changes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence of minerals crystallizing from magma, from olivine to quartz.

tossups.p: Olivine crystals wrapped in rims of pyroxene record a step in this sequence, in which an early mineral reacts with the leftover melt and starts turning into the next one. Minerals far apart in this sequence are rarely found together in the same rock.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that shows the order in which minerals form as magma cools, ending with quartz.

tossups.p: Going down one branch of this sequence, each mineral’s silicon–oxygen tetrahedra are linked more fully than in the mineral before it: first as separate units, then in single chains, then in double chains, and finally in sheets.
tossups.r: That discontinuous branch runs from olivine to biotite mica. For 10 points, name this sequence of minerals crystallizing from cooling magma.

tossups.p: At the Carnegie Institution’s Geophysical Laboratory in Washington, D.C., this sequence’s namesake heated samples in a furnace, cooled them to set temperatures, and then quickly quenched them to see which crystals had formed at each step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence, worked out by a Canadian scientist, that lists the order in which minerals crystallize from magma.

tossups.p: Read in reverse, this sequence explains partial melting: when a rock is heated, the minerals at the bottom of this sequence melt first, so the first melt is richer in silica than the rock it came from.
tossups.r: Read forward, it begins with olivine. For 10 points, name this sequence that shows the order in which minerals crystallize from magma.

tossups.p: One branch of this sequence starts with anorthite and ends with albite, because the same crystals slowly trade calcium for sodium as the magma around them cools. Those two minerals are the end members of the plagioclase feldspars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence that shows which minerals crystallize first and last from cooling magma.

tossups.p: Dense crystals that form early in this sequence, such as olivine, can sink to the floor of a magma chamber, a process called crystal settling. Removing those early crystals leaves the remaining melt richer in silica, in a process called fractional crystallization.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Y-shaped sequence of minerals that crystallize from magma, ending with quartz.

tossups.p: Because the first and last minerals in this sequence form at such different temperatures, an igneous rock rarely contains both of them. Heated together, those two minerals react to make pyroxene, the mineral that comes second on one branch of this sequence.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence in which olivine crystallizes first and quartz crystallizes last from cooling magma.

tossups.p: Minerals from the middle of this sequence, like hornblende and plagioclase containing both calcium and sodium, build intermediate rocks such as andesite and diorite. Minerals from the very top of this sequence build ultramafic rocks such as peridotite.
tossups.r: Its bottom minerals build light, felsic rocks like granite. For 10 points, name this sequence of crystallizing minerals.

tossups.p: Augite crystallizes before hornblende on one branch of this sequence, where each mineral reacts with the surrounding liquid to become a mineral with a brand-new crystal structure. That branch is called discontinuous.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence, which begins with olivine and ends with quartz, showing how minerals crystallize from magma.

tossups.p: This sequence was explained in the 1928 book _The Evolution of the Igneous Rocks_, whose author argued that removing early crystals from a basalt magma could leave behind a melt that would harden into granite-like rock.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence, named for a Canadian scientist, that lists the order in which minerals crystallize from magma.

tossups.p: Biotite, a dark mica, is the last mineral on one branch of this sequence, while muscovite, a light mica, crystallizes after its two branches join, just before the final mineral. Both of those micas split into thin, flexible sheets.
tossups.r: Diagrams of it look like a letter Y. For 10 points, name this sequence of minerals that crystallize from cooling magma, starting with olivine and ending with quartz.

tossups.p: The dark, ferromagnesian minerals on the left side of this sequence are rich in iron and magnesium, which is why rocks built from its early minerals, like basalt, are dark. The right side of this sequence holds plagioclase feldspar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Y-shaped sequence that shows the order in which minerals crystallize from cooling magma.

tossups.p: This sequence explains why dark basalt is full of pyroxene and calcium-rich plagioclase, while pale granite is rich in quartz and potassium feldspar. Its high-temperature minerals are rich in iron and magnesium, and its low-temperature minerals are rich in silica.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sequence, worked out by a Canadian scientist, in which olivine crystallizes first and quartz last.

trap.title: Crystallizing, not weathering
trap.body: The Goldich dissolution series lists almost the same minerals in almost the same order, with olivine at one end and quartz at the other, but it ranks how fast minerals weather at Earth’s surface, not how they crystallize from magma. Fractional crystallization is the process of removing early crystals, which this series helps explain, but it is a different answer. Players also hear “olivine” or “quartz” and blurt out a mineral instead of the whole series.
trap.fix: Cooling magma, crystallizing, high and low temperatures, a Y-shaped chart, and continuous and discontinuous branches mean Bowen’s reaction series. Weathering, dissolving, and stability at Earth’s surface mean the Goldich dissolution series. Saying only “reaction series” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bowen’s reaction series (accept Bowen’s series; prompt on reaction series; do not accept “Goldich dissolution series”)

topics.name: Olivine
topics.kicker: Olive-green magnesium iron silicate · Most common mineral of the upper mantle
topics.briefing: Olivine is a glassy, olive-green mineral made of magnesium, iron, silicon, and oxygen. It is one of the first minerals to crystallize when magma cools, and it is the most common mineral in Earth’s upper mantle. Its crystals turn Hawaii’s Papakōlea Beach green, its gem form, peridot, is August’s birthstone, and some of its crystals have even fallen to Earth inside meteorites.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: About 410 kilometers below the surface, the crushing pressure of the mantle squeezes this mineral into a denser form called wadsleyite, which makes seismic waves suddenly speed up at that depth. Deeper still, it changes again into ringwoodite.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green magnesium iron silicate, whose gem form is peridot.

tossups.p: In 2014, scientists described a tiny diamond from Brazil that had trapped a speck of ringwoodite, a high-pressure form of this mineral, and that speck held water. The find suggested that rock hundreds of kilometers down in the mantle may hold a lot of water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this olive-green mineral, the most common mineral in Earth’s upper mantle.

tossups.p: Seawater reacting with this mineral in mantle rock exposed on the ocean floor makes serpentine and releases hydrogen gas, a process called serpentinization. That process helps power the Lost City, a field of tall white chimneys near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green mineral, a magnesium iron silicate whose gem variety is peridot.

tossups.p: Pallasites, stony-iron meteorites named for the German scientist Peter Simon Pallas, hold glassy green crystals of this mineral set in shiny iron-nickel metal. Thin, polished slices of those meteorites glow like stained glass when light shines through them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral whose gem form, peridot, is the birthstone for August.

tossups.p: NASA’s Stardust mission brought home dust from Comet Wild 2 [“VILT two”] that held crystals of this mineral, which must have formed at very high temperatures near the young Sun. That surprised scientists who expected comets to hold only icy, never-heated material.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this olive-green silicate mineral, the first to crystallize in Bowen’s reaction series.

tossups.p: Spacecraft have found this mineral spread widely across Mars, which suggests that much of that planet’s surface has stayed dry for a very long time, because water breaks this mineral down quickly. On Earth, this mineral is one of the first to weather away.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green magnesium iron silicate whose gem variety, peridot, is the birthstone for August.

tossups.p: Some scientists have proposed grinding up this mineral and spreading it on beaches or farm fields, because as it weathers, it pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. This mineral’s magnesium ends up in the carbonate compounds that form.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green magnesium iron silicate, the most common mineral in the upper mantle.

tossups.p: Gems of this mineral were mined in ancient times on Zabargad, an Egyptian island in the Red Sea also called St. John’s Island. Much of the world’s supply of those gems later came from the San Carlos Apache Reservation in Arizona.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral whose gem form, peridot, is the birthstone for August.

tossups.p: This mineral forms orthorhombic crystals with poor cleavage, breaking instead along curved, shell-like surfaces, and it rates about 6.5 to 7 on the Mohs scale. Its color darkens as more iron takes the place of magnesium in its crystals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this glassy green silicate mineral, whose gem form is peridot.

tossups.p: Dunite, a rock made almost entirely of this mineral, is named for New Zealand’s Dun Mountain, whose rocks weather to a dull brown. Peridotite, the rock that makes up most of the upper mantle, is also made mostly of this mineral.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this green silicate mineral, the most common mineral in Earth’s upper mantle.

tossups.p: In this mineral, each silicon–oxygen tetrahedron stands alone, linked to the others only through magnesium and iron ions, so it is classified as a nesosilicate. Its magnesium-rich form has such a high melting point that it is used in bricks that line furnaces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this glassy, olive-green mineral whose gem form, peridot, is August’s birthstone.

tossups.p: This mineral forms a continuous series between magnesium-rich forsterite and iron-rich fayalite [“FAY-uh-lite”]. Its chemical formula is written with magnesium and iron sharing two places, alongside one silicon atom and four oxygen atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this olive-green silicate, the most common mineral in Earth’s upper mantle, whose gem form is peridot.

tossups.p: This mineral sits at the top of the Goldich dissolution series, because it breaks down faster than any other common silicate at Earth’s surface. It is rarely found together with quartz, because the two react at high temperatures to make pyroxene.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mineral, the first to crystallize from cooling magma in Bowen’s reaction series.

tossups.p: Papakōlea Beach, near the southern tip of Hawaii’s Big Island, gets its unusual green sand from crystals of this mineral that wore out of an old volcanic cinder cone. Because those crystals are heavy, waves carry lighter grains away and leave them behind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this olive-green mineral, the most common mineral in Earth’s upper mantle, whose gem form is peridot.

tossups.p: This mineral is common in dark, mafic igneous rocks like basalt and gabbro, but it is rare in granite. It is made of magnesium, iron, silicon, and oxygen, and its glassy grains are often green.
tossups.r: Its gem form, peridot, is August’s birthstone. For 10 points, name this mineral named for its olive-green color.

trap.title: Mineral, gem, or rock?
trap.body: Olivine, peridot, and peridotite sound alike and show up in the same tossups. Peridot is only the gem form of this mineral, so saying it earns a prompt, while peridotite is a whole rock, made mostly of olivine, that forms the upper mantle. Forsterite and fayalite are the two end members of the olivine series, so naming one of them is not the same as naming the mineral.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this mineral,” say olivine. A rock that makes up the upper mantle is peridotite, and a birthstone or gem by itself is peridot. Green, glassy, first in Bowen’s reaction series, and weathering fastest all point to olivine.
trap.line: Real answer line: Olivine (prompt on peridot; do not accept “peridotite”)

topics.name: Salinity
topics.kicker: How salty water is · The ocean averages about 35 parts per thousand
topics.dates: Ocean average: about 35 parts per thousand
topics.briefing: Salinity measures how much salt is dissolved in water. A kilogram of average seawater holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts, mostly sodium and chloride, which works out to about 3.5 percent. Evaporation makes water saltier and rain makes it fresher, and in the Dead Sea, nearly ten times saltier than the ocean, swimmers bob like corks.
topics.answerHtml: Salinity (accept saltiness, salt content, or salt concentration; prompt on salt; do not accept “density” or “salinization”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Johan Georg Forchhammer and Alexander Marcet found that the main dissolved substances in seawater keep nearly the same ratios to one another everywhere, even though this property changes from place to place. That rule is called the principle of constant proportions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how much salt is dissolved in water, which averages about 35 parts per thousand in the ocean.

tossups.p: William Dittmar analyzed seawater samples collected on the voyage of HMS _Challenger_ and confirmed that sodium, chloride, and other ions keep fixed ratios even when this property changes. Chloride makes up more than half of the dissolved material this property measures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of seawater, the amount of salt in it, which goes up when water evaporates.

tossups.p: Since 1978, oceanographers have reported this property on a unitless “practical” scale based on how well seawater conducts electricity compared with a standard solution of potassium chloride. Instruments called CTDs measure conductivity, temperature, and depth to find it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of water, the amount of dissolved salt it contains.

tossups.p: Before electronic sensors, oceanographers found this property by first measuring chlorinity, adding silver nitrate to seawater to see how much chloride it held. The Danish physicist Martin Knudsen helped set up that method around 1900.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which averages about 35 parts per thousand in the open ocean.

tossups.p: NASA’s Aquarius instrument, launched in 2011 aboard an Argentine satellite, mapped this property across the sea surface by sensing faint microwaves given off by the water. Europe’s SMOS satellite has also measured this property from orbit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of seawater, which rises when water evaporates and leaves its salt behind.

tossups.p: Thousands of drifting robots called Argo floats sink as deep as 2,000 meters and then rise, recording temperature and this property along the way. Together, those two measurements let scientists work out the density of the water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how salty water is, usually given in parts per thousand.

tossups.p: Because evaporation removes more water than rivers and rain add, the Mediterranean Sea is higher in this property than the Atlantic, so its dense water spills out beneath the Atlantic water flowing in at the Strait of Gibraltar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of the dissolved salt in seawater, which averages about 35 parts per thousand.

tossups.p: In 1715, Edmond Halley suggested that the age of Earth could be estimated by measuring how fast this property of lakes and the ocean goes up. John Joly later tried that idea using the sodium carried to the sea by rivers, but his answer was far too young.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how much salt is dissolved in water, which evaporation raises and rain lowers.

tossups.p: Euryhaline animals, like salmon and bull sharks, can survive big changes in this property, while stenohaline animals cannot. Bull sharks have been found far up freshwater rivers like the Mississippi, and salmon move between salty oceans and freshwater rivers during their lives.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of water, which in the open ocean averages about 35 parts per thousand.

tossups.p: In a salt-wedge estuary, like the mouth of the Mississippi River, dense seawater slides upstream beneath the river’s fresh water, so this property is much higher near the bottom. Water with an in-between value of this property is called brackish.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how much salt is dissolved in water.

tossups.p: When sea ice forms in Antarctica’s Weddell Sea, it leaves most of its salt behind in the water below, a process called brine rejection that raises this property. That cold, dense water sinks to form Antarctic Bottom Water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property of seawater that, along with temperature, controls its density and drives the thermohaline circulation.

tossups.p: A layer of the ocean where this property changes quickly with depth is called a halocline, and lines on a map that connect places with equal values of this property are called isohalines.
tossups.r: Evaporation raises it, and rain lowers it. For 10 points, name this measure of the salt dissolved in seawater.

tossups.p: In the open ocean, this property is highest at the sea surface in the subtropics, about 20 to 30 degrees from the equator, where dry air lets evaporation outpace rainfall. It is lower near the rainy equator and near melting polar ice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of how salty seawater is, which averages about 35 parts per thousand.

tossups.p: Raising this property lowers the temperature at which water freezes, so ocean water stays liquid a little below 0 °C. Raising it also makes water conduct electricity better, which is how most modern instruments measure it.
tossups.r: The Dead Sea’s value is nearly ten times the ocean’s. For 10 points, name this measure of how salty water is.

tossups.p: Rivers slowly add to this property of the ocean by carrying in ions weathered out of rocks on land, and gases from volcanoes add chloride. Sodium and chloride ions make up most of the dissolved material that this property measures.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this measure of the salt in seawater, which averages about 35 parts per thousand.

trap.title: Saltiness, not density
trap.body: Thermohaline-circulation tossups describe cold, salty water sinking, so players blurt out “density,” which depends on both temperature and this property and is a different answer. A halocline is only a layer where this property changes quickly, and “salinization” means salt building up in soil. Saying just “salt” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: Parts per thousand, PSU, conductivity sensors, evaporation raising it, and the Dead Sea mean salinity. Mass per volume or kilograms per cubic meter mean density, and a layer of fast change means halocline (salt) or thermocline (temperature).
trap.line: Real answer line: Salinity (accept saltiness or salt content; prompt on salt; do not accept “density”)

topics.name: Earth’s magnetic field
topics.kicker: Made by molten iron in the outer core · Steers compasses and shields the planet
topics.dates: Last full reversal: about 780,000 years ago
topics.briefing: Deep below your feet, swirling molten iron in Earth’s outer core works like a giant electric generator, wrapping the planet in a magnetic field. That field is why a compass needle points north, and it shields Earth from the solar wind, steering some of its particles toward the poles to light up the auroras. Every so often the field flips, and the last full reversal came about 780,000 years ago.
topics.answerHtml: Earth’s magnetic field (accept geomagnetic field or geomagnetism; prompt on plain magnetic field; do not accept “magnetosphere” or “Van Allen belts”)
accept: the magnetic field of the earth

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his _Dream Pool Essays_ of 1088, Shen Kuo described a magnetized needle that pointed not due south but slightly east of south, one of the earliest records of the gap between true direction and the direction set by this field. That gap is now called declination.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, produced in the outer core, that compass needles line up with.

tossups.p: In 1701, Edmond Halley published a chart of the Atlantic Ocean with curved lines joining places where compass needles pointed the same amount away from true north, the first map of its kind for this field. Lines where that difference is zero are called agonic lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, made by swirling molten iron in the outer core, that steers compass needles.

tossups.p: In the 1830s, Carl Friedrich Gauss and Wilhelm Weber set up a network of observatories to track this field, and Gauss used mathematics to show that it comes almost entirely from inside the planet. An older unit named for Gauss is still used to measure it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, created by molten iron in the outer core, that makes compass needles point north.

tossups.p: In 1581, the English compass maker Robert Norman showed that a balanced, magnetized needle tips downward, pointing into the ground, because of this field. That angle, called inclination or dip, reaches 90 degrees at two places on the surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, created in the outer core, whose effects include the northern lights.

tossups.p: In 1831, James Clark Ross reached a spot on the Boothia Peninsula in northern Canada where a dip needle pointed straight down, the first time anyone had found the northern pole of this field. That pole has since wandered across the Arctic Ocean toward Siberia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, made in the planet’s outer core, which compass needles line up with.

tossups.p: In 1909, Edgeworth David, Douglas Mawson, and Alistair Mackay hauled sledges over the Antarctic ice to become the first people to reach the southern pole of this field, during Ernest Shackleton’s _Nimrod_ expedition.
tossups.r: This field funnels charged particles from the Sun toward the poles. For 10 points, name this field that steers compass needles.

tossups.p: In 1906, Bernard Brunhes found volcanic rocks in France that were magnetized in the opposite direction from the present field, and in 1929, Motonori Matuyama proposed that this field had flipped in the distant past. The last full flip came about 780,000 years ago.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, generated by the outer core, that compass needles follow.

tossups.p: Geologists divide the last few million years into long stretches called chrons, named Brunhes, Matuyama, Gauss, and Gilbert, according to which way this field pointed. Matching stripes of rock on both sides of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge record those flips.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, which has reversed many times and which compass needles line up with.

tossups.p: During the Laschamp event, about 41,000 years ago, this field weakened sharply and briefly swung far from its usual direction before recovering, an episode called an excursion rather than a full reversal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, which protects the planet from the solar wind and makes compass needles point north.

tossups.p: Satellites and the International Space Station pass through the South Atlantic Anomaly, a region over South America and the South Atlantic where this field is weakest, so charged particles dip closer to the planet and can cause computer glitches.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, which traps charged particles in the Van Allen belts.

tossups.p: During the Carrington Event of 1859, a blast of charged particles from the Sun shook this field so hard that telegraph wires sparked and auroras were seen near the tropics. A similar storm in 1989 knocked out electric power across Quebec.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, created by molten iron in the outer core, that steers compass needles.

tossups.p: On the side facing the Sun, the solar wind slows sharply at a bow shock in front of this field, while on the night side the solar wind stretches this field into a long tail. The boundary where this field’s push balances the wind is the magnetopause.
tossups.r: The region it controls is the magnetosphere. For 10 points, name this field that steers compass needles.

tossups.p: In 1995, Gary Glatzmaier and Paul Roberts ran a computer model of churning liquid metal that flipped this field all on its own, supporting the idea that a dynamo in the outer core creates it.
tossups.r: Sea turtles and many birds sense it to find their way. For 10 points, name this field, which compass needles line up with.

tossups.p: William Gilbert’s 1600 book _De Magnete_ argued that the whole planet acts like a giant magnet, which he modeled with a small lodestone sphere called a terrella, or “little Earth.” Gilbert showed that a compass needle dips near the poles of that sphere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, generated by molten iron in the outer core, that compass needles line up with.

tossups.p: The northern pole of this field is, in physics terms, a south magnetic pole, which is why it attracts the north end of a compass needle. That pole lies in the Arctic, but it has slowly wandered toward Siberia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this field, made by swirling molten iron in the outer core, that funnels solar particles toward the poles to make auroras.

trap.title: Say whose field
trap.body: This answer is packed with physics words, so players blurt out plain “magnetic field,” which is a separate, general Physics answer here and earns only a prompt. Others buzz with one of its parts or effects: the magnetosphere (the region of space it controls), the Van Allen belts (the particles it traps), the auroras, or the outer core that makes it.
trap.fix: Say “Earth’s magnetic field” or “geomagnetic field,” and if you get a prompt, add “Earth’s.” Compasses pointing north, reversals, magnetic stripes on the seafloor, declination, and the geodynamo point here. Teslas, solenoids, and right-hand rules with no mention of the planet mean the general magnetic field.

topics.name: Troposphere
topics.kicker: Lowest layer of the atmosphere · Where nearly all weather happens
topics.dates: From the ground to roughly 10 km up (higher over the equator)
topics.briefing: The troposphere is the bottom layer of Earth’s atmosphere, the one we live and breathe in. It holds about three-quarters of all the air and nearly all of the water vapor, so almost every cloud, raindrop, and storm happens here. Its air usually gets colder the higher you climb, which is why snow can sit on mountaintops all summer.
topics.answerHtml: Troposphere (prompt on atmosphere or lower atmosphere; do not accept “tropopause” or “stratosphere”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This layer’s name comes from a Greek word meaning “turning,” because its air is always churning and mixing. Around 1902, Léon Teisserenc de Bort’s instrument-carrying balloons showed that the air stops getting colder at the top of this layer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where nearly all weather happens.

tossups.p: In the International Standard Atmosphere, this layer ends at a height of 11 kilometers, where the air has cooled to −56.5 °C. Its real top ranges from less than 10 kilometers up over the poles to more than 15 kilometers over the equator.
tossups.r: Its temperature usually falls about 6.5 °C per kilometer. For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere.

tossups.p: Over the equator, this layer reaches its greatest height, and the air at its top can be colder than −70 °C, even colder than the air at its top over the poles. Over the poles, this layer is much thinner.
tossups.r: Its top boundary is the tropopause. For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, where weather happens.

tossups.p: A bubble of rising, unsaturated air in this layer cools by about 10 °C for every kilometer it climbs, a value called the dry adiabatic lapse rate, while saturated air cools more slowly because condensing water vapor releases heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the atmosphere closest to the ground, home to nearly all clouds and storms.

tossups.p: Giant meanders in the high winds of this layer, called Rossby waves after Carl-Gustaf Rossby, steer storms and can stall into blocking patterns that cause long heat waves. Jet streams blow near the top of this layer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where temperature usually drops with height.

tossups.p: As greenhouse gases have built up, scientists have measured this layer warming while the layer above it cools, a pattern that points to those gases rather than the Sun as the cause. This layer holds nearly all of the atmosphere’s water vapor, the greenhouse gas that traps the most heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, found just below the stratosphere, where nearly all weather happens.

tossups.p: In December 1952, a temperature inversion trapped coal smoke near the ground in this layer over London, creating the Great Smog and leading to Britain’s Clean Air Act of 1956. In an inversion, warm air sits on top of cooler air instead of below it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer we live in, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere.

tossups.p: Rising air in this layer cools until it reaches its dew point at the lifting condensation level, which marks the flat bottoms of puffy cumulus clouds. Towering thunderheads in this layer can grow all the way to its top, where they spread out into anvil shapes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this weather layer, the lowest layer of the atmosphere, which holds most of the air’s mass.

tossups.p: Air pressure falls to about half of its sea-level value roughly 5.5 kilometers up in this layer, at the 500-millibar level that forecasters watch on weather maps. Climbers on Mount Everest, whose summit lies inside this layer, breathe air at about one-third of sea-level pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where temperature usually drops as you climb.

tossups.p: In 1735, George Hadley explained the steady trade winds with a giant loop of air rising near the equator, all within this layer. In the loops now named Hadley cells, the air sinks back down at around 30 degrees latitude.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, which holds nearly all of its water vapor.

tossups.p: The lowest part of this layer, called the boundary layer, feels friction from the ground, which slows the wind and makes it gusty near the surface. On sunny days the boundary layer grows thicker as the warmed ground stirs up the air above it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where nearly all weather happens.

tossups.p: Only about 10 percent of Earth’s ozone is found in this layer, where near the ground it is a harmful pollutant in smog, formed when sunlight acts on car exhaust and factory fumes.
tossups.r: This layer lies just below the stratosphere. For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, where clouds and storms form.

tossups.p: Long-distance jet airliners usually cruise near the top of this layer, where the air is thin and fast winds called jet streams can speed them along or slow them down. The summit of Mount Everest sits inside this layer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, where temperature drops with height.

tossups.p: This layer holds about three-quarters of the mass of the whole atmosphere and nearly all of its water vapor. It is warmed mostly from below, by sunlight that heats the ground, so warm air near the surface rises and stirs it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where nearly all weather happens.

tossups.p: Twice a day, weather stations around the world release balloons carrying radiosondes, which radio back temperature, humidity, and wind as they rise through this layer and beyond. Its name comes from a Greek word for “turning,” since its air is always mixing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest layer of the atmosphere, where nearly all weather and clouds occur.

clues.t: The lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere, where we live, directly below the stratosphere
Where nearly all weather happens and most clouds form
Temperature usually drops as you go up, by about 6.5 °C per kilometer (the lapse rate)
Its top boundary is called the tropopause
Holds about three-quarters of the atmosphere’s mass and nearly all of its water vapor
Its name comes from a Greek word for “turning,” because its air is always churning and mixing
Thickest over the equator (more than 15 km) and thinnest over the poles (less than 10 km)
Warmed mostly from below by sun-heated ground, so warm air near the surface rises and stirs it
Jet streams blow near its top, where long-distance airliners usually cruise
A temperature inversion, warm air on top of cooler air, can trap smog near the ground
Mount Everest’s summit lies inside it, where air pressure is about one-third of sea level’s
Léon Teisserenc de Bort’s instrument-carrying balloons found where it ends, around 1902
In the International Standard Atmosphere, it ends 11 km up, where the air is −56.5 °C
Over the equator its top is highest and can be colder than −70 °C, colder than its top over the poles
Rising unsaturated air cools about 10 °C per km (the dry adiabatic lapse rate); saturated air cools more slowly
Rossby waves, named for Carl-Gustaf Rossby, are giant meanders in its high winds that steer storms
As greenhouse gases build up, it warms while the stratosphere above it cools
An inversion caused London’s Great Smog (1952), which led to Britain’s Clean Air Act of 1956
Rising air reaches its dew point at the lifting condensation level, which marks the flat bases of cumulus clouds
Air pressure is about half of sea level’s roughly 5.5 km up, at the 500-millibar level
George Hadley (1735) explained the trade winds with a loop of rising air; in Hadley cells, air sinks near 30° latitude
Its lowest part, the boundary layer, feels friction from the ground and grows thicker on sunny days
Holds only about 10 percent of Earth’s ozone; near the ground, ozone is a harmful pollutant in smog
Radiosondes carried by weather balloons, launched twice a day, measure its temperature, humidity, and wind
Thunderheads can grow all the way to its top and spread into anvil shapes

trap.title: Layer, not its lid
trap.body: The tropopause is only the boundary at the top of this layer, and the stratosphere is the next layer up, home of the ozone layer. Both are different answers, and their look-alike names make a fast buzz risky. Saying only “atmosphere” earns a prompt, so be ready to name the layer.
trap.fix: Remember the order going up: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere. Weather, clouds, water vapor, and temperature falling with height mean the troposphere; ozone and temperature rising with height mean the stratosphere. A boundary where the temperature stops falling is the tropopause.
trap.line: Real answer line: Troposphere (prompt on atmosphere; do not accept “tropopause” or “stratosphere”)

topics.name: Coriolis effect
topics.kicker: Apparent sideways push caused by Earth’s spin · Makes hurricanes rotate
topics.briefing: Because Earth spins, anything moving a long way across its surface, like wind, an ocean current, or a long-range artillery shell, seems to curve: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis worked out the math of this effect in 1835, and it is why hurricanes spin. It is far too weak to decide which way a toilet flushes, though.
topics.answerHtml: Coriolis effect (accept Coriolis force or Coriolis acceleration; prompt on fictitious force or inertial force; do not accept “centrifugal force”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1651, the Italian astronomers Giovanni Battista Riccioli and Francesco Grimaldi argued that if Earth spun, this effect would push cannonballs sideways, and because they saw no such push, they concluded that Earth stands still.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force that deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: Pierre-Simon Laplace [“luh-PLAHS”] included a term for this effect in his tidal equations of 1778, more than 50 years before the French engineer it is named for wrote about it. For horizontal motion, this effect is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect of Earth’s rotation that makes hurricanes spin and bends the trade winds.

tossups.p: In 1835, a French engineer studying the energy of rotating machines, such as waterwheels, worked out the math of this effect, which appears only to observers in a spinning frame of reference. It is called a fictitious force because nothing actually pushes the moving object.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: In 1856, the American meteorologist William Ferrel used this effect to explain how Earth’s spin bends the great wind belts, and a middle-latitude circulation cell is named for him. This effect turns the trade winds so that they blow from the northeast and southeast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force caused by Earth’s rotation, which deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: Buys Ballot’s law says that if you stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, low pressure is on your left, a rule that works because this effect turns winds sideways. Christophorus Buys Ballot published that rule in 1857.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that makes storms spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: During the voyage of the _Fram_, Fridtjof Nansen noticed that sea ice drifted at an angle to the right of the wind, and in 1905 Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained that drift using this effect. Ekman showed that ocean currents twist into a spiral with depth.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect of Earth’s spin that deflects moving water and air.

tossups.p: In 1962, Ascher Shapiro of MIT let a large, carefully settled tank of water sit undisturbed before draining it, and the resulting whirlpool turned counterclockwise because of this effect. In ordinary sinks and toilets, this effect is far too weak to decide which way the water swirls.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, caused by Earth’s rotation, that makes hurricanes spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: When the Rossby number of a moving system is small, as in large storms or ocean currents, this effect is important, but in small systems like a bathtub drain it can be ignored. Its strength depends on how fast an object moves and on the sine of its latitude.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force, named for a French engineer, that is caused by Earth’s rotation.

tossups.p: The Eötvös effect, which makes an object moving east weigh slightly less and one moving west weigh slightly more, is the vertical part of this effect. It is named for the Hungarian physicist Loránd Eötvös.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force caused by Earth’s spin, which deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: Mass flow meters named for this effect measure how much fluid passes through a vibrating tube by detecting the tiny twist the moving fluid causes. Flies sense this effect with knob-like organs called halteres [“hal-TEER-eez”], which help them balance in flight.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which on Earth deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: Pilots can feel a dizzying illusion named for this effect if they tilt their heads while their plane is turning, because the motion confuses the balance organs in their inner ears. Spinning chairs used to train pilots can trigger the same illusion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force that bends winds and ocean currents on the rotating Earth.

tossups.p: High above the ground, geostrophic winds blow parallel to the lines of equal pressure on a weather map, because the pull toward low pressure is balanced by this effect. Near the ground, friction slows the wind and weakens this effect, so winds cut across those lines toward low pressure.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect of Earth’s spin that makes storms turn counterclockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.

tossups.p: This effect is too weak within about 5 degrees of the equator to start a storm spinning, so hurricanes almost never form there. Ocean gyres turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere partly because of this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that deflects moving objects to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

tossups.p: At the equator, tour guides sometimes stage a trick in which water seems to drain clockwise on one side of a painted line and counterclockwise on the other, falsely blaming this effect. Long-range artillery and snipers really do have to correct for this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force caused by Earth’s rotation, which makes hurricanes spin.

tossups.p: A ball rolled straight across a spinning merry-go-round seems to curve to the riders, a classic way to show this effect. On Earth, this effect bends the trade winds and the ocean’s great currents.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this apparent force that deflects moving objects to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.

clues.t: Deflects moving air and water to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
Caused by Earth’s rotation; it appears only when motion is viewed from a spinning frame
Makes hurricanes spin counterclockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere
Named for a French engineer who worked out its math in 1835
For horizontal motion, it is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles
A “fictitious” or inertial force: nothing actually pushes the object, but its path seems to curve
Turns the trade winds so they blow from the northeast and southeast
Helps turn ocean gyres clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere
Far too weak to decide which way sinks and toilets drain; equator “demonstrations” of opposite swirls are tricks
Too weak within about 5 degrees of the equator to start storms spinning, so hurricanes almost never form there
Balances the pull toward low pressure in geostrophic winds, which blow parallel to isobars
Ekman transport: it turns wind-driven surface water to the right of the wind in the Northern Hemisphere
A ball rolled across a spinning merry-go-round seems to curve to the riders
Long-range artillery and snipers must correct for it
Riccioli and Grimaldi (1651) argued that a spinning Earth would push cannonballs sideways; seeing no push, they said Earth stands still
Pierre-Simon Laplace’s tidal equations (1778) already included a term for it
Its namesake worked out its math while studying the energy of rotating machines like waterwheels
William Ferrel (1856) used it to explain the great wind belts; the Ferrel cell is named for him
Buys Ballot’s law (1857): with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere, low pressure is on your left
Fridtjof Nansen saw sea ice drift to the right of the wind on the _Fram_; Vagn Walfrid Ekman explained it in 1905
Ascher Shapiro (MIT, 1962) showed that a carefully settled tank in the Northern Hemisphere drains counterclockwise
It matters when the Rossby number is small, as in big storms and ocean currents
Its acceleration is twice Earth’s spin rate times the velocity (a cross product); its strength depends on the sine of latitude
The Eötvös effect, its vertical part, makes objects moving east weigh slightly less
Mass flow meters named for it detect the twist that moving fluid gives a vibrating tube
Flies sense it with knob-like balance organs called halteres
Pilots who tilt their heads during a turn can feel a dizzying illusion named for it

trap.title: Coriolis or centrifugal?
trap.body: Both are “fictitious” forces that show up in spinning frames, so tossups about rotation can mean either one. Centrifugal force pushes things outward, away from the axis, even when they sit still, while this effect pushes only on things that are moving, sideways to their motion. Ekman transport and geostrophic winds are results of this effect, not the effect itself.
trap.fix: Moving air or water bending right in the Northern Hemisphere, hurricanes spinning, the trade winds, or a French engineer from 1835 means the Coriolis effect. Riders pressed against the wall of a spinning ride, or anything flung outward, means centrifugal force. Saying only “fictitious force” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Coriolis effect (accept Coriolis force; prompt on fictitious force; do not accept “centrifugal force”)

topics.name: Ozone layer
topics.kicker: Shield of three-atom oxygen in the stratosphere · Blocks most UV light
topics.dates: Discovered 1913 by Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson
topics.briefing: About 15 to 35 kilometers above your head floats an invisible sunscreen: the ozone layer. Ozone is a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule instead of two, and it soaks up most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet light. In 1985, scientists reported a giant “hole” in the layer over Antarctica caused by CFC chemicals, and the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased those chemicals out.
topics.answerHtml: Ozone layer (accept ozone or ozonosphere; accept O3 or trioxygen; prompt on ozone hole; do not accept “stratosphere” or “oxygen”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1881, Walter Noel Hartley measured how the gas in this layer absorbs light, and he proposed that it explains why sunlight reaching the ground has almost no light with wavelengths shorter than about 300 nanometers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the stratosphere that shields life from most of the Sun’s ultraviolet rays.

tossups.p: In 1913, the French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson discovered this layer high in the atmosphere by measuring how strongly sunlight was dimmed at certain wavelengths. Fabry is also known for the Fabry–Pérot interferometer, a tool for measuring light.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, made of a three-atom form of oxygen, that blocks most of the Sun’s ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: Gordon Dobson built a spectrophotometer in the 1920s to measure this layer, and the unit used for its thickness is named for him. If all of this layer were squeezed down to sea-level pressure, it would be only about 3 millimeters thick.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this protective layer in the stratosphere that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: In 1930, Sydney Chapman explained how this layer forms: ultraviolet light splits oxygen molecules into single atoms, which then join with other oxygen molecules. Ultraviolet light also breaks the resulting molecules apart again, in a never-ending cycle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the stratosphere that blocks most of the Sun’s harmful UV rays.

tossups.p: Although most of the gas in this layer is made high above the tropics, the slow Brewer–Dobson circulation carries it toward the poles, so this layer is usually thicker at high latitudes than over the equator.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, about 15 to 35 kilometers up, that shields Earth from ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: Christian Friedrich Schönbein [“SHURN-bine”] named the gas that makes up this layer in 1840, from a Greek word meaning “to smell,” because of the sharp odor it gives off near electric sparks. The same smell can hang in the air after a lightning storm.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, made of a three-atom form of oxygen, that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet rays.

tossups.p: In 1928, Thomas Midgley Jr. helped invent refrigerant gases that seemed perfectly safe, and he once breathed one in and blew out a candle with it to prove the point. Decades later, scientists learned that those gases drift high into the sky and destroy this layer.
tossups.r: Those gases are called CFCs. For 10 points, name this layer that shields Earth from ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: James Lovelock’s electron capture detector found the gases that harm this layer in air samples from all over the world, including on a ship voyage to Antarctica in the early 1970s. Those gases, invented as refrigerants, last for decades in the air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the stratosphere, thinned by CFCs, that blocks most ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: In 1974, Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland warned that chlorine from refrigerator and spray-can gases could destroy this layer, work that won them the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry along with Paul Crutzen. One chlorine atom can break down as many as 100,000 of this layer’s molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, about 15 to 35 kilometers up, that shields Earth from ultraviolet rays.

tossups.p: In 1985, Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner, and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey reported a startling springtime drop in this layer, using decades of measurements from their Halley research station.
tossups.r: That “hole” appears over Antarctica every year. For 10 points, name this layer that blocks most of the Sun’s ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: In 1986, Susan Solomon led an expedition to McMurdo Station and helped show that icy polar stratospheric clouds speed up the chemical reactions that destroy this layer each spring. Those clouds form only in the bitter cold of the polar winter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, thinned by CFCs, that shields life on Earth from ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: The 1985 Vienna Convention set up a framework to protect this layer, and in 2009 that convention and the treaty that followed it became the first United Nations treaties ratified by every member country. The UN marks September 16, that treaty’s signing date, as an international day for this layer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, protected by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: The 2016 Kigali Amendment added HFCs to a treaty first written to protect this layer, because those replacement gases, though harmless to this layer, trap heat as powerful greenhouse gases.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer of the stratosphere, damaged by CFCs, that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet light.

tossups.p: Halons, gases once widely used in fire extinguishers, contain bromine, which destroys this layer even faster than chlorine does, so they were phased out along with the pesticide methyl bromide. Like chlorine, bromine is set free when sunlight breaks those gases apart far above the ground.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this layer, found mostly in the stratosphere, that absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet rays.

tossups.p: This layer blocks nearly all of the Sun’s UV-C light and most of its UV-B light, but it lets most UV-A light through. Near the ground, the same gas that forms this layer is a harmful pollutant in smog.
tossups.r: This layer sits in the stratosphere. For 10 points, name this layer that protects living things from sunburn-causing ultraviolet rays.

Found mostly in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 kilometers up

A “hole” in it opens over Antarctica every spring

About 90 percent of its gas is in the stratosphere; near the ground, the same gas is a harmful pollutant in smog
Icy polar stratospheric clouds and the polar vortex help chlorine destroy it over Antarctica
Blocks nearly all UV-C and most UV-B light, but lets most UV-A through
Discovered in 1913 by the French physicists Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson
Walter Noel Hartley (1881) found that its gas absorbs UV, explaining why sunlight at the ground lacks the shortest UV wavelengths
Gordon Dobson built a spectrophotometer to measure it in the 1920s
Mostly made over the tropics, but the Brewer–Dobson circulation carries it poleward, so it is thicker at high latitudes

The 2016 Kigali Amendment added HFCs, replacement gases that are harmless to it but trap heat
Halons in fire extinguishers contain bromine, which destroys it even faster than chlorine

trap.title: Not the whole stratosphere
trap.body: This layer is only part of the stratosphere, the second layer of the atmosphere, and the stratosphere is a separate answer here. Clues about chlorofluorocarbons, the Montreal Protocol, and the Antarctic “hole” tempt players to answer with those instead, and plain “oxygen” is wrong too, since this gas has three atoms per molecule, not two.
trap.fix: If the question asks for the thin band of gas that absorbs ultraviolet light, say ozone layer (plain “ozone” is fine too). If it asks for the whole layer between the troposphere and the mesosphere, say stratosphere. Saying “ozone hole” earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ozone layer (accept ozone; prompt on ozone hole; do not accept “stratosphere”)

topics.name: Upwelling
topics.kicker: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface · Feeds great fisheries
topics.dates: Peaks off California in spring and summer
topics.briefing: Upwelling happens when wind pushes the ocean’s warm surface water away from a coast and cold, deep water rises to take its place. That deep water is full of nutrients, so tiny plankton bloom and feed huge schools of fish, which is why upwelling zones off Peru and California are some of the richest fishing grounds on Earth. It even helps make San Francisco’s famous summer fog.
topics.answerHtml: Upwelling (accept coastal upwelling or equatorial upwelling; do not accept “downwelling,” “Ekman transport,” or “El Niño”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1802, Alexander von Humboldt measured the surprisingly cold sea along the west coast of South America, where this process keeps the water chilly, and the cold current there now bears his name. Seabirds feeding in those rich waters left huge piles of droppings on offshore islands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rising of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean’s surface, which makes the coasts of Peru and California so rich in fish.

tossups.p: In the 1800s, workers mined mountains of seabird droppings called guano on the Chincha Islands, left by birds that ate fish made plentiful by this process. That guano was shipped around the world as fertilizer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which wind-driven currents bring cold, nutrient-rich water up from the deep ocean.

tossups.p: Cold water carried by the Cromwell Current rises to the surface west of the Galápagos Islands in this process, letting Galápagos penguins live farther north than any other wild penguins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that brings cold, nutrient-rich deep water up to the ocean’s surface, feeding rich fisheries.

tossups.p: Every summer, strong monsoon winds blowing along the coasts of Somalia and Oman drive this process in the Arabian Sea, cooling the surface water and feeding huge blooms of plankton. The same summer winds carry heavy rains to India.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process, the opposite of downwelling, in which cold, deep water rises to the surface.

tossups.p: A hurricane’s winds can churn up cold water behind the storm through this process, leaving a cool trail called a cold wake that can weaken a second storm following the same path.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which cold, deep water rises to the sea surface, often along coasts where wind pushes surface water away.

tossups.p: Cold water brought up by this process in the Benguela Current helps keep Namibia’s coast dry and foggy, and some beetles in the Namib Desert survive by drinking fog droplets that collect on their backs. Chile’s Atacama Desert has the same kind of cold coast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rising of cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean, which also feeds rich fisheries off southwestern Africa.

tossups.p: Fast-growing diatoms, algae with glassy shells, usually dominate the plankton blooms fed by this process, because it brings up plenty of nitrates, phosphates, and silica from below. Those blooms feed small fish, like sardines and anchovies, that bigger fish and seabirds eat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that supports some of the world’s richest fisheries by lifting cold, deep water to the surface.

tossups.p: In 1972, the anchoveta fishery, then the largest fishery in the world, collapsed when a strong El Niño weakened this process, on top of years of heavy fishing. Before the crash, boats had been landing millions of tons of the small fish each year, mostly to grind into fishmeal.
tossups.r: During El Niño, weak trade winds let warm water cover the coast of Peru. For 10 points, name this rising of cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface.

tossups.p: On the Great Lakes, a strong offshore wind can trigger this process, so the water at a Lake Michigan beach can turn several degrees colder in a single day. Along ocean coasts, this process can keep beach water surprisingly cold even in summer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which deep, cold water rises to replace surface water pushed away by wind.

tossups.p: Satellites that measure sea-surface temperature and the green color of chlorophyll spot this process as cold, plankton-rich patches of water along the western coasts of continents, such as off northwest Africa in the Canary Current.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that brings nutrient-rich deep water up to the ocean’s surface.

tossups.p: Around Antarctica, strong winds that circle the continent drive this process, lifting deep water that has been away from the surface for centuries and feeding the krill that whales eat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the deep ocean, the opposite of downwelling.

tossups.p: Cold water brought up by this process along the California coast chills the air above it, helping create San Francisco’s famous summer fog. This process there is strongest in spring and summer, when winds blow south along the coast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that brings cold, nutrient-rich water up from the deep ocean.

tossups.p: Along the equator in the eastern Pacific, the trade winds push surface water away to the north and south, so cold water rises in this process and forms a cool tongue of water stretching west from South America.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rising of deep ocean water, which El Niño weakens.

tossups.p: Because of the Coriolis effect, wind blowing along a coast moves the surface water at a right angle to the wind, a motion called Ekman transport. When that motion carries surface water away from the shore, this process replaces it from below.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process that brings cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface off places like Peru and California.

tossups.p: This process is strongest in four big ocean currents along the western edges of continents: the California, Humboldt, Canary, and Benguela currents. Zones where it happens cover only a small part of the ocean but provide a large share of the world’s fish catch.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this process in which cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to the ocean’s surface.
