Fast-growing diatoms, algae with glassy silica shells, dominate its plankton blooms
In 1972 the anchoveta fishery, then the world’s largest, collapsed during a strong El Niño and years of heavy fishing
Offshore winds can trigger it on the Great Lakes, chilling Lake Michigan beach water within a day
Satellites spot it as cold, chlorophyll-rich patches along western coasts, like the Canary Current off northwest Africa
Off California it is strongest in spring and summer, when winds blow south along the coast

trap.title: Upwelling, El Niño, or Ekman?
trap.body: El Niño tossups also mention Peru, anchovies, and the trade winds, but El Niño is the warm event that shuts this process off. Ekman transport is the sideways push of surface water that causes this process, and downwelling is its opposite, where surface water sinks. Naming any of them loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Cold, nutrient-rich water rising to the surface, rich fisheries, and coastal fog mean upwelling. Warm water spreading east and the Southern Oscillation mean El Niño; water moving at a right angle to the wind means Ekman transport; and sinking surface water means downwelling.
trap.line: Real answer line: Upwelling (accept coastal upwelling; do not accept “downwelling” or “El Niño”)

topics.name: Faults
topics.kicker: Breaks in the crust where rock slips past rock · Where earthquakes start
topics.dates: Elastic rebound theory: Harry Fielding Reid, 1910
topics.briefing: Faults are breaks in Earth’s crust where the rock on one side has moved past the rock on the other, sometimes by a few centimeters and sometimes by many kilometers over millions of years. When stress builds up along a stuck fault and the rock suddenly lurches, the ground shakes in an earthquake. California’s San Andreas Fault, where two tectonic plates grind sideways past each other, caused the great San Francisco earthquake of 1906.
topics.answerHtml: Faults (accept fault lines or fault zones; accept specific types such as normal, reverse, thrust, or strike-slip faults; prompt on fractures or cracks; do not accept “earthquakes” or a single named example like “San Andreas Fault”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Miners gave the two sides of these features their names: they could hang lanterns from the block above a slanted one while standing on the block below it. In one kind of these features, that upper block slides downward as the crust is stretched apart.
tossups.r: That kind is called normal, and the two blocks are called the hanging wall and the footwall. For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust along which blocks of rock move.

tossups.p: Polished, grooved surfaces called slickensides form where rock grinds against rock along these features, and their scratches show which way the rock slid. Crushed, powdery rock called gouge often fills the zones along them.
tossups.r: Earthquakes begin when rock suddenly slips along one. For 10 points, name these fractures in Earth’s crust, whose main types are normal, reverse, and strike-slip.

tossups.p: Geologists describe the orientation of one of these features with two measurements: its strike, the compass direction of the line where it meets level ground, and its dip, the angle at which it slants downward. The dip-slip kinds of these features move up or down along that slant.
tossups.r: Strike-slip kinds move sideways instead. For 10 points, name these breaks in rock, such as California’s San Andreas, along which earthquakes happen.

tossups.p: After studying the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, Harry Fielding Reid proposed elastic rebound theory, which says rock on both sides of one of these features slowly bends as stress builds, then snaps back when the rock suddenly slips.
tossups.r: That 1906 earthquake struck along the San Andreas. For 10 points, name these fractures in Earth’s crust where blocks of rock move past each other.

tossups.p: By the principle of cross-cutting relationships, one of these features must be younger than any rock layers it slices through. Matching layers on opposite sides of one of these features often sit at different heights, because the rock has shifted along it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust, which come in normal, reverse, and strike-slip types.

tossups.p: In Montana’s Glacier National Park, a huge slab of ancient rock slid over much younger rock along the Lewis Overthrust, and Chief Mountain is a lone leftover piece of that slab. That overthrust formed as the crust was squeezed and one block was shoved up and over another.
tossups.r: Low-angle reverse types like it are called thrusts. For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust along which rock slips during earthquakes.

tossups.p: Because moderate earthquakes had struck Parkfield, California, about every 22 years, scientists predicted another one there by 1993, but it did not arrive until 2004. Parkfield sits on the most famous of these features in the United States.
tossups.r: That feature, the San Andreas, marks where two plates slide past each other. For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust where earthquakes occur.

tossups.p: The University of California’s football stadium in Berkeley was built right across the Hayward example of these features, which slowly creeps and pulls curbs and walls out of line. The Hayward example also produced a large earthquake in 1868.
tossups.r: California’s most famous example is the San Andreas. For 10 points, name these cracks in Earth’s crust along which blocks of rock slip.

tossups.p: The 1994 Northridge earthquake near Los Angeles struck on a “blind” one of these features, which lies buried and never breaks the ground surface. It was a thrust, a kind of these features that forms where the crust is squeezed together.
tossups.r: Other kinds include normal and strike-slip. For 10 points, name these fractures along which rocks move, causing earthquakes.

tossups.p: Nevada’s Basin and Range region is a series of raised blocks called horsts and dropped blocks called grabens [“GRAH-bunz”], created as the crust stretched apart along these features. Wyoming’s Teton Range rose along one of them at its eastern edge.
tossups.r: Those are the normal type, in which the hanging wall drops down. For 10 points, name these breaks in rock along which earthquakes happen.

tossups.p: Turkey’s North Anatolian example of these features has produced a series of major earthquakes, including one near Izmit [“IZ-mit”] in 1999. Its two sides slide horizontally past each other, with the far side moving to the right, so geologists call it right-lateral.
tossups.r: California’s San Andreas is also a right-lateral, strike-slip example. For 10 points, name these fractures in Earth’s crust where rock slips during earthquakes.

tossups.p: Wallace Creek, on California’s Carrizo [“kuh-REE-zoh”] Plain, takes a sharp sideways jog where it crosses one of these features, because the ground has shifted along it over thousands of years. Low spots along such features can fill with water to form sag ponds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust, such as the San Andreas, which come in normal, reverse, and strike-slip types.

tossups.p: In 1965, J. Tuzo Wilson named the transform type of these features, which offset mid-ocean ridges into staggered segments. Where a transform type cuts across land, as in California, its two sides slide horizontally past each other.
tossups.r: Earthquakes strike when rock lurches along these features. For 10 points, name these fractures, including the San Andreas, along which blocks of rock move.

tossups.p: Engineers set the Trans-Alaska Pipeline on sliding supports where it crosses the Denali example of these features, so when a magnitude 7.9 earthquake shifted the ground there in 2002, the pipeline did not break.
tossups.r: That quake moved the ground mostly sideways. For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust, whose types include normal, reverse, and strike-slip, along which earthquakes happen.

tossups.p: Tension, which pulls the crust apart, makes the hanging wall of one of these features slide down, while compression pushes the hanging wall up compared with the footwall. Shear stress makes the two blocks slide sideways past each other instead.
tossups.r: Those motions define the normal, reverse, and strike-slip types. For 10 points, name these breaks in Earth’s crust, such as the San Andreas, where earthquakes start.

clues.t: Breaks in Earth’s crust where blocks of rock have moved past each other
Earthquakes happen when stress builds up and the rock along one suddenly slips
Three main types: normal, reverse, and strike-slip
California’s San Andreas is the most famous example, where the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other
The block above a slanted one is the hanging wall; the block below it is the footwall
Normal type: tension stretches the crust apart and the hanging wall slides down
Reverse type: compression squeezes the crust and pushes the hanging wall up
A thrust is a low-angle reverse type that can shove older rock on top of younger rock
Strike-slip type: shear stress makes the blocks slide horizontally; the San Andreas is right-lateral
Elastic rebound theory: rock on both sides bends as stress builds, then snaps back when it slips
Where the crust stretches, normal ones create raised horsts and dropped grabens, as in Nevada’s Basin and Range
Transform types offset mid-ocean ridges and form transform plate boundaries
Where one breaks the ground surface, it can leave a step-like cliff called a scarp
Miners named the two walls: they hung lanterns on the hanging wall and stood on the footwall
Polished, grooved slickensides show which way the rock slid; crushed rock called gouge fills the zone
Orientation given by strike (compass direction along level ground) and dip (the angle it slants down)
Cross-cutting relationships: one is younger than any rock layers it cuts through
Harry Fielding Reid proposed elastic rebound theory after studying the 1906 San Francisco earthquake
Parkfield, California, on the San Andreas: a quake predicted by 1993 finally came in 2004
The Lewis Overthrust in Glacier National Park slid ancient rock over younger rock; Chief Mountain is a leftover piece
The 1994 Northridge earthquake struck on a buried “blind” thrust
The Hayward example creeps beneath the University of California’s football stadium in Berkeley and caused an 1868 earthquake
Turkey’s North Anatolian is a right-lateral strike-slip example that caused the 1999 Izmit earthquake
Wallace Creek on the Carrizo Plain jogs sideways across the San Andreas; sag ponds fill low spots along such breaks
J. Tuzo Wilson named the transform type in 1965
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline crosses the Denali example on sliding supports and survived a 2002 earthquake there
Wyoming’s Teton Range rose along a normal one at its eastern edge

trap.title: Fault or earthquake?
trap.body: Fault tossups are packed with earthquake clues, like elastic rebound, the 1906 San Francisco quake, and Parkfield, so players blurt out “earthquakes,” which names the shaking, not the crack in the rock. Others name one famous example, like the San Andreas, or one part, like the hanging wall, when the question wants the whole category.
trap.fix: Listen for “these features,” “these breaks,” or “these fractures,” and answer faults. Naming a type, such as normal, thrust, or strike-slip faults, is fine, and “fractures” alone earns a prompt. Save “earthquakes” for questions about the shaking and its waves.
trap.line: Real answer line: Faults (accept fault lines or specific types such as strike-slip faults; prompt on fractures; do not accept “earthquakes” or “San Andreas Fault”)

topics.name: Jurassic period
topics.kicker: Middle period of the Mesozoic Era · Age of Stegosaurus and giant sauropods
topics.briefing: The Jurassic period, from about 201 to 145 million years ago, was the middle part of the Mesozoic Era, when giant long-necked dinosaurs like Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus roamed among ferns, cycads, and conifers. It is named for the Jura Mountains between France and Switzerland, and its rocks in Germany preserved Archaeopteryx, one of the earliest known birds. Meanwhile, the supercontinent Pangaea was breaking apart.
topics.answerHtml: Jurassic period (prompt on Mesozoic Era; do not accept “Triassic,” “Cretaceous,” or “Jurassic Park”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Albert Oppel helped found the use of fossil zones by dividing this period’s rock layers into zones, each marked by a different kind of ammonite. European geologists traditionally split this period’s rocks into three parts called the Lias, the Dogger, and the Malm.
tossups.r: Alexander von Humboldt named its limestone for the Jura Mountains. For 10 points, name this middle period of the Mesozoic Era.

tossups.p: Mary Anning dug ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons out of seaside cliffs at Lyme Regis, part of an English World Heritage coastline that is named for this period. Those marine reptiles swam in the shallow seas that covered much of Europe during this period.
tossups.r: On land, Stegosaurus and Allosaurus lived late in this period. For 10 points, name this period of the Mesozoic Era, about 201 to 145 million years ago.

tossups.p: In 1824, William Buckland named Megalosaurus, the first dinosaur to receive a scientific name, from bones found in English rocks from the middle of this period. Christopher Wren built St. Paul’s Cathedral from Portland stone, a limestone that formed late in this period.
tossups.r: This period followed the Triassic. For 10 points, name this period whose name comes from the Jura Mountains.

tossups.p: In 1861, a skeleton of Archaeopteryx [“ar-kee-OP-ter-iks”], a feathered animal with teeth and a long bony tail, was found in Germany’s Solnhofen [“ZOHLN-hoh-fen”] limestone, which formed late in this period. The same limestone preserved the small dinosaur Compsognathus and the pterosaur Pterodactylus.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this middle period of the Mesozoic Era, which came between the Triassic and the Cretaceous.

tossups.p: Enormous volcanic eruptions in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, which broke out as Pangaea began to split apart, are blamed for the mass extinction that opened this period. With many rivals gone, dinosaurs took over the land during this period.
tossups.r: This period ended about 145 million years ago, when the Cretaceous began. For 10 points, name this period that followed the Triassic.

tossups.p: The Morrison Formation, a set of rock layers spread across the western United States, holds many dinosaur fossils from late in this period, including the bones at Dinosaur National Monument. Allosaurus, the state fossil of Utah, was a top predator in the Morrison.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this period between the Triassic and the Cretaceous, whose name comes from a European mountain range.

tossups.p: The spiked tail of Stegosaurus, a plant-eater from this period, is nicknamed a “thagomizer” after a joke in Gary Larson’s comic _The Far Side_. Stegosaurus shared the land with giant long-necked sauropods like Diplodocus.
tossups.r: Archaeopteryx also lived in this period. For 10 points, name this period that followed the Triassic, named for mountains on the border of France and Switzerland.

tossups.p: Fossils from shale near Holzmaden, Germany, show that ichthyosaurs living early in this period gave birth to live young in the sea instead of laying eggs. Some of those fossils even preserve the outline of the ichthyosaurs’ skin.
tossups.r: Plesiosaurs and pterosaurs also lived in this period. For 10 points, name this period, about 201 to 145 million years ago.

tossups.p: During this period, the supercontinent Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south, and the central Atlantic Ocean began to open between North America and Africa. Warm, shallow seas flooded the edges of the continents.
tossups.r: Stegosaurus and Brachiosaurus lived late in this period. For 10 points, name this period between the Triassic and the Cretaceous.

tossups.p: Forests of conifers, cycads, ginkgoes, and tree ferns covered the land during this period, before flowering plants became common. Huge plant-eating sauropods such as Diplodocus fed on that greenery, and no large ice sheets covered the poles.
tossups.r: Archaeopteryx, an early bird, lived near this period’s end. For 10 points, name this period, the middle part of the Mesozoic Era.

tossups.p: The honey-colored stone of England’s Cotswold Hills and the city of Bath is oolitic limestone, built from tiny rounded grains that look like fish eggs, which formed in warm, shallow seas during this period. The name “oolite” comes from Greek words for “egg stone.”
tossups.r: On land, this period’s dinosaurs included Allosaurus and Stegosaurus. For 10 points, name this period that followed the Triassic.

tossups.p: In 1903, Elmer Riggs named Brachiosaurus [“brak-ee-uh-SOR-us”], or “arm lizard,” from bones found in western Colorado, because its front legs were longer than its back legs. Riggs called it the largest known dinosaur, and it lived late in this period.
tossups.r: Archaeopteryx and Stegosaurus also lived in this period. For 10 points, name this middle period of the Mesozoic Era.

tossups.p: During the “Bone Wars” against his rival Edward Drinker Cope, Othniel Charles Marsh named Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, and Diplodocus in the late 1870s from fossils of animals that lived during this period. His crews also dug up many of this period’s dinosaurs at Como Bluff in Wyoming.
tossups.r: This period came between the Triassic and the Cretaceous. For 10 points, name this period, about 201 to 145 million years ago.

tossups.p: The Kimmeridge Clay, a dark rock layer laid down late in this period, is the main source rock for the oil pumped from beneath the North Sea. Its name comes from a village on England’s Dorset coast.
tossups.r: Stegosaurus lived on land at the same time. For 10 points, name this period named for the Jura Mountains.

tossups.p: Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, and the giant Brachiosaurus all lived during this period, while ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs swam in its seas and the early bird Archaeopteryx lived on islands in present-day Germany. Pangaea broke apart during this period.
tossups.r: Michael Crichton named a 1990 novel about cloned dinosaurs for this period. For 10 points, name this middle period of the Mesozoic Era.

Lasted from about 201 to 145 million years ago
Named for the Jura Mountains on the border of France and Switzerland

Home to Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Brachiosaurus, and Diplodocus
Archaeopteryx, a feathered early bird with teeth, lived late in it; a skeleton was found in Germany’s Solnhofen limestone in 1861

Conifers, cycads, ginkgoes, and ferns filled its forests; flowering plants were not yet common
Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs swam in its seas, and pterosaurs flew overhead
Ammonites are index fossils used to divide its rocks into zones

Albert Oppel split its rocks into ammonite zones; traditional European names for its three parts are Lias, Dogger, and Malm
Mary Anning found ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons at Lyme Regis, on an English World Heritage coast named for it
William Buckland named Megalosaurus (1824), the first dinosaur to get a scientific name, from English rocks of this age
Christopher Wren built St. Paul’s Cathedral from Portland stone, a limestone from late in it
Oolitic limestone (Greek for “egg stone”) of the Cotswolds and Bath formed in its warm seas
Eruptions in the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province are blamed for the extinction at its start
The Morrison Formation of the western U.S., including Dinosaur National Monument, holds its late dinosaurs
Allosaurus, a top predator from late in it, is Utah’s state fossil
Stegosaurus’s spiked tail is nicknamed the “thagomizer,” from a _Far Side_ cartoon
Othniel Charles Marsh named Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, and Diplodocus in the 1870s, during the Bone Wars with Edward Drinker Cope
Elmer Riggs named Brachiosaurus (“arm lizard”) in 1903 from bones found in western Colorado

trap.title: Jurassic or Cretaceous?
trap.body: Many famous dinosaurs did not live in the Jurassic. Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, and Velociraptor all lived in the later Cretaceous, even though they star in a movie named for this period, and the first dinosaurs appeared earlier, in the Triassic. Saying “Mesozoic” names the whole era, and naming the book or movie is wrong too.
trap.fix: Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus, Archaeopteryx, the Jura Mountains, and Pangaea splitting apart mean the Jurassic. Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, flowering plants, and the asteroid impact mean the Cretaceous; the first dinosaurs and Pangaea still mostly in one piece mean the Triassic. If you say “Mesozoic,” expect a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Jurassic period (prompt on Mesozoic; do not accept “Triassic” or “Cretaceous”)
